findings.title: Breaking API change: order() added as abstract method
findings.body: The new int order() method is added to the CryptoProvider interface as an abstract method with no default implementation. Any third-party implementation of CryptoProvider will fail to compile against this SPI. A default (e.g., `default int order() { return 100; }`) would preserve existing implementations while letting the in-tree providers (Default/FIPS/Elytron at 200, AuthzClient at 100) override it as needed. As-is, every external CryptoProvider consumer must be updated simultaneously.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default JDK provider, not BouncyCastle
findings.body: The implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which on a stock JVM is SUN/SunJSSE/SunPKCS11 — not BouncyCastle. The method is named `getBouncyCastleProvider()` and the other implementations (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider) genuinely return a BC-based provider, so callers expecting BC algorithms/properties on the returned Provider will silently get something else. Either return null (matching WildFlyElytronProvider) or add a BC provider lookup, and document the contract.

findings.title: Dead code: ASN1Encoder instances are created and discarded
findings.body: Lines 114-115 invoke `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger)` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger)` but never call `toByteArray()` nor capture the return value. The actual conversion happens in the immediately following `writeDerSeq(...)`, which constructs two brand-new encoders from the same BigIntegers. The two discarded encoder allocations plus two BigInteger-to-byte-array serializations are pure waste and look like a copy-paste mistake; they should be removed.

findings.title: readSequence silently returns empty for indefinite-length encoding
findings.body: If `readLength()` returns -1 (the indefinite-length form per X.690), the loop condition `while (length > 0)` is never entered (since -1 > 0 is false) and an empty `List` is returned without raising an error. DER forbids indefinite-length encoding, so encountering it indicates a malformed or non-DER input — silently returning an empty list masks the bug and lets the caller continue processing a bogus signature. The method should throw IOException when `length == -1`.

findings.title: Test only verifies round-trip conversion, not signature correctness
findings.body: The test signs data with the JDK provider, converts DER → RS → DER → RS via AuthzClientCryptoProvider, and asserts the two RS arrays match. It never checks that the resulting R/S actually correspond to the signature's real R and S components — a bug that swaps R/S, off-by-ones a byte, or always returns zeros would pass this test. Add an assertion that re-assembles a Signature from the converted bytes and runs `signature.verify()` against the original data and public key; also test negative cases (tampered DER, wrong length).
